lead: Photodetector noise sets the smallest signal a receiver can trust. Shot noise comes from the random arrival of carriers, so it grows with the photocurrent and the dark current. Thermal noise comes from the load resistor and does not depend on the light at all. The two add as powers, and their ratio to the signal power is the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which tells you whether a receiver is shot-noise limited or thermal-noise limited. Only a few universities teach this as a topic of its own.
prereq: You need responsivity from Detection principles and the gain M and excess noise factor F from Avalanche photodiodes.

sections.h3: Shot noise, dark current and thermal noise

blocks.text: Current is a stream of separate electrons. A steady 1 µA is about 6.2 × 10¹² electrons per second, each arriving at a random moment (Poisson statistics), so the current flickers about its mean. This is shot noise. Its mean-square value grows with the current and with the bandwidth B of the receiver after the photodiode (the electrical bandwidth, not the optical frequency).
i<sub>sh</sub>² is the mean-square shot-noise current in A²; q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; I<sub>p</sub> is the photocurrent and I<sub>d</sub> the dark current, both in A; B is in Hz. This is the PIN form.

Dark current is the current that flows with no light: carriers made by heat in the depleted volume (the bulk part, I<sub>db</sub>) plus leakage along the surface of the chip (I<sub>ds</sub>). In an APD the bulk dark current passes through the gain region and is multiplied, while the surface leakage goes around it and is not. So the APD output dark current is MI<sub>db</sub> + I<sub>ds</sub>, and the APD shot noise is
M is the avalanche gain and F the excess noise factor. Put M = F = 1 for a PIN to get back the first formula.

Thermal (Johnson) noise is the random motion of electrons in the load resistor R<sub>L</sub>. It is there with no light at all, and it is set by the resistor, the temperature and the bandwidth. A real amplifier adds its own noise, often written as an amplifier noise figure F<sub>n</sub> that multiplies the thermal term.
k<sub>B</sub> = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant, T the temperature in K and R<sub>L</sub> the load resistance in Ω.

sections.h3: Adding noise and the signal-to-noise ratio

blocks.text: The noise sources are independent, so their mean squares (powers) add: σ² = i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>², where σ is the total rms noise current. Never add rms currents: 5.07 nA and 40.7 nA give √(5.07² + 40.7²) = 41.0 nA, not 45.8 nA.
I<sub>p</sub>² is the signal power (as a mean-square current) and σ² the total noise power, both in A². For an APD the signal is (MI<sub>p</sub>)².

Two limits are worth knowing. Thermal-noise limited: SNR ≈ I<sub>p</sub>²R<sub>L</sub>/(4k<sub>B</sub>TB). Since I<sub>p</sub> ∝ P, the SNR grows as P²: 10 dB more optical power gives 20 dB more SNR. Shot-noise limited: SNR ≈ I<sub>p</sub>/(2qB), which grows only as P: 10 dB more power gives 10 dB more SNR. The two terms are equal when I<sub>p</sub>R<sub>L</sub> = 2k<sub>B</sub>T/q, which is 51.7 mV at 300 K. So a PIN with a 1 kΩ load is thermal-noise limited until I<sub>p</sub> reaches about 52 µA, far more than a receiver normally sees.

A larger RL lowers thermal noise but raises the RLC time constant and so narrows the bandwidth; this is the problem of Optical receiver structure and sensitivity. Low-frequency 1/f noise also exists below a few kilohertz, but it is negligible at data rates.
Datasheets give the noise as a power per root hertz. Divide the noise mean square by B to get the noise spectral density in A²/Hz; its square root is in A/√Hz.

blocks.where: NEP is the noise equivalent power in W/√Hz: the optical power that would give SNR = 1 in a 1 Hz bandwidth. σ/√B is the rms noise current per root hertz in A/√Hz and R the responsivity in A/W. A smaller NEP means a quieter detector.

blocks.text: For the 1 kΩ load at 300 K, √(4k<sub>B</sub>T/R<sub>L</sub>) = 4.07 pA/√Hz; with R = 0.8 A/W, NEP = 5.09 pW/√Hz. Over B = 100 MHz the power for SNR = 1 is NEP × √B = 5.09 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁴ = 50.9 nW.

examples.question: A PIN receiver has responsivity R = 0.8 A/W, received power P = 1 µW, dark current I<sub>d</sub> = 1 nA, bandwidth B = 100 MHz and load R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ at T = 300 K. Find the rms shot noise, the rms thermal noise, the total rms noise and the SNR. Is the receiver shot-noise or thermal-noise limited?
steps: Photocurrent: I<sub>p</sub> = RP = 0.8 × 1 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.800 µA; I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>d</sub> = 0.801 µA.
Shot noise: i<sub>sh</sub>² = 2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.801 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁸ = 2.57 × 10⁻¹⁷ A²; rms 5.07 nA.
Thermal noise: i<sub>th</sub>² = 4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 10⁸/1000 = 1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵ A²; rms 40.7 nA.

Thermal noise is 1.656 × 10⁻¹⁵/2.57 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 64 times the shot noise, so the receiver is thermal-noise limited. Check with the crossover: I<sub>p</sub> = 0.8 µA is far below 2k<sub>B</sub>T/(qR<sub>L</sub>) = 51.7 µA.
examples.answer: Shot noise 5.07 nA rms, thermal noise 40.7 nA rms, total 41.0 nA rms, SNR = 381 (25.8 dB); the receiver is thermal-noise limited.

traps: Adding rms noise currents. Add the mean squares, then take one square root.
Leaving the dark current out of the shot-noise term.
In an APD, multiplying all of the dark current by M²F. Only the bulk part is multiplied; surface leakage adds 2qI<sub>ds</sub>B unmultiplied.
Treating a bigger R<sub>L</sub> as free. It lowers thermal noise but raises R<sub>L</sub>C and narrows the bandwidth.
Quoting SNR(dB) as 20 log₁₀ of the power ratio. SNR here is already a ratio of mean squares (powers), so use 10 log₁₀.

quiz.q: Write the PIN shot-noise formula and define every symbol.
quiz.a: i<sub>sh</sub>² = 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>d</sub>)B: q electron charge, I<sub>p</sub> photocurrent, I<sub>d</sub> dark current, B electrical bandwidth.

quiz.q: Why are noise powers added rather than rms currents?
quiz.a: Independent random currents have variances that add. The total rms is √(i<sub>sh</sub>² + i<sub>th</sub>²), which is less than the sum of the rms values.

quiz.q: A PIN has R = 1.0 A/W, P = 2 µW, I<sub>d</sub> = 0, B = 50 MHz, R<sub>L</sub> = 2 kΩ, T = 300 K. Give both mean-square noise currents and say which dominates.
quiz.a: Shot: 2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 5 × 10⁷ = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷ A². Thermal: 4 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 × 5 × 10⁷/2000 = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁶ A². Thermal noise is about 13 times larger and dominates.

quiz.q: Why does SNR rise 20 dB for each 10 dB of optical power when thermal noise dominates, but only 10 dB when shot noise dominates?
quiz.a: Thermal-limited SNR ∝ I<sub>p</sub>² ∝ P², so a factor 10 in P gives 100 in SNR (20 dB). Shot-limited SNR = I<sub>p</sub>/(2qB) ∝ P, so a factor 10 in P gives 10 in SNR (10 dB).

quiz.q: An APD has M = 10, F = 5, primary current I<sub>p</sub> = 1 µA (dark current negligible) and B = 100 MHz. Find the mean-square shot noise.
Define NEP and give its unit.
quiz.a: The optical power that gives SNR = 1 in a 1 Hz bandwidth: NEP = (σ/√B)/R, in W/√Hz.

quiz.q: Name the two parts of the dark current and say how APD gain affects each.
quiz.a: Bulk dark current, generated in the depleted volume, passes through the gain region and is multiplied by M. Surface leakage current bypasses the gain region and is not multiplied.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coherent receivers mix the signal with a strong local laser, which lifts the signal above thermal noise so the receiver reaches the shot-noise limit. Transimpedance amplifier design is about the amplifier's own input noise current and voltage, not just one resistor. Optical preamplifiers add signal–spontaneous beat noise, which then dominates both terms in this chapter. Search next for "input-referred noise current", "shot-noise-limited detection" and "signal-spontaneous beat noise".

figure.caption: SNR of the worked example's PIN receiver (R = 0.8 A/W, B = 100 MHz, R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ) as the power changes. At 1 µW it is 25.8 dB and follows the thermal limit; the shot limit takes over only above about −12 dBm, where the two noise powers are equal.

spec.aria: SNR in decibels against received power from minus 50 to 0 dBm. The solid curve follows a dashed thermal-limit line of slope 20 dB per 10 dB at low power and bends towards a dashed shot-limit line of slope 10 dB per 10 dB near minus 12 dBm. A point marks 25.8 dB at minus 30 dBm.
